utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My apologies. I was delayed on another matter, and so we are late starting. Mr. Djurdjic, I understand there's some matter that you need to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have a few questions, actually two questions, one pertaining to the transcript, and the second one is information from the Prosecution that we received

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I wonder if this matter should not be addressed in private session rather than in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the concern, that we have witnesses that have some protective measures? Is that the concern?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, the concern has to do with -- and the specific issue that's being raised by my colleague and some filings that have been made with respect to these witnesses which are of a confidential nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. Well, in that case, we better go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we have 92 ter resolved for the moment. There may, of course, be some oral evidence led from the witness in addition to any past statement or transcript, if there's need for some amplification or clarification, and that's what the 92 ter allows. If we can move then to the other issue, Mr. Djurdjic. The counsel for the Prosecution tells us that in fact each of the -- eight of the nine future witnesses to be called in the next two weeks have been the subject of notification to the Defence, and I have here notifications dated the 16th of February and the 23rd of February, which appear to set out those witnesses, eight of the nine. The one omitted is the witness (redacted) And do I understand correctly, or do you accept that you had notification of eight of the nine witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to be clear, in the latest notification from the Prosecution, all is timely. We have no objections to that, except for that part that has to do with the subpoena. So we don't know if that order will stay or not. This is one of the concerns of the Defence. As for this gentleman, I don't know if it's a private session matter or not. It doesn't matter. I'm not going to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: (redacted) Some of them are not on the list. That is why we thought this gentleman whose last name you mentioned, that there's only five days left. We were informed yesterday that he is due on Monday. So this is part of the whole problem of the order and whether the order will remain so that we have an opportunity to prepare. I don't know if you understood me, but there was -- we did not receive any decision granting the request of the Prosecution for subpoenas. The Prosecution did inform us about their plans for the following two weeks. That part of it is all right. It's just that this witness was not on a regular list for two weeks in advance but in an addition that had to do with the subpoena request. So I think that even then there was a question of whether these witnesses would be able to come or not. Thank you very much. I don't want to take up any more of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we could go back to private session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would be grateful, Ms. Kravetz, if you would prepare now and serve on the Defence and provide a copy to the Chamber of the witnesses that it is contemplated will be called from this point on, including the witnesses who are listed for the week commencing the 9th of March, so that there is a clear list in the order that you anticipate calling them. And if there is a particular date requirement about any witness on that list, if that could be indicated. In other words, if travel or other -- or subpoena or other issues dictate the witness being called on a particular day or around a particular date, please indicate that because that may affect the order in which that witness comes to be called. But if we can get that, it will then be clear to the Defence and the Chamber just what is proposed and in what order, and preparations can be made accordingly. And if a bit of luck and with the goodwill of the Defence, it may be that the matter can proceed then without further difficulty. I'd be grateful. Is there any other matter, then, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have some transcript issues, Your Honour, but as for the other issue, we will make our full contribution, and we have accepted to always have lined up a reserve witness, as it were. But I think when we received the schedule for March, I did not notice that there was a single free day, because every week the schedule was for five days a week. But under the current conditions and with the resources that we have at our disposal, I assure you that even doing our best, we are unable to meet this schedule unless we proceed in the manner that you have just now proposed, and I thank you for that. Now, I would like to touch upon the transcript of Monday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is that the transcript is inaccurate, it would be a practical first measure to just note in writing to the Registry your concern of inaccuracy, and the transcript can then be checked. Is that the concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Maybe I have misspoken. There are not -- it's not incorrect, the transcript. There's just a letter that needs to be added there. But as for the other matter, I would just like to ask of the witness, because the word was entered in the transcript in Serbian, and it wasn't translated into English. So it's not really a transcript correction, Your Honour. There are not errors in the transcript. It is just that the letters P and B have been replaced for a name of a village, and as for the other two words, I would just -- I hope you will allow me to ask of the witness to clarify those two words and translate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the only complaint with the transcript being the transposition of the letter P and a B in the name of a village, I think will have been extremely successful. The sorts of problems that you have identified are matters that can be taken up with the Registry who will arrange corrections, if necessary, in the formal transcript. Could I mention before it passes without comment, that you have on more than one occasion, both yourself and Mr. Djordjevic, mentioned that you as a Defence feel yourselves under time pressures. That is a matter which needs to be taken up with the Registry if it is your concern that the resources presently available to you are inadequate. We are progressing, as originally indicated, to a timetable which in the coming month will usually be five days a week, and that will be our expectation of progress for the future. There will, of course, be reasons for interruption, and every now and again we must effect a break to enable everybody to catch up a few days. But we can expect a normal progression of five days a week sitting. Now, if that is a matter that is presenting undue difficulty to you and Mr. Djordjevic, that's a matter that must be discussed with the Registry officers to see what, if anything, change can be made, because that is the timetable that you will need to anticipate. I believe now -- is there something further?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just want to make this clear, completely. Mr. Djordjevic had a discussion with the Registry last week, and he assessed it as very positive, so now we expect that the Trial Chamber or, rather, that someone from the Registry should get in touch with the Trial Chamber, Your Honour, to reassess the level that has been assigned to this case, and I think they will seek your opinion. My understanding was that this will be done in the course of this week. So the procedure before the Registry is already underway and I expect that it will be resolved in a positive manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So long as you're clear that decisions about the funding of the Defence are in the hands of the Registry and not of the Chamber. That is the way it will proceed. I think we now need to go into private session so that the witness can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: First of all I'd like to ask you, how is your health? Are you all right? You have to say it into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not too well, but I think I'll manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear you. There's something wrong with this headset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will speak for a moment to see whether you are hearing. Are you able to hear now the translation of what I say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear the Judge, but I do not hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only hear the Judge speaking in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has just told me that he can hear you, he can hear you speaking in English, but he cannot hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear anything that the Judge said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He is receiving on the earphone the English translation -- the translation into B/C/S of what I am saying. If you are speaking in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now. Now I can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can we resume now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your health problems, are they chronic, or is it something that you just have now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, I had flew here and then I got sick, and then yesterday I had some personal, private, problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, we were a bit too fast the last time we spoke, so please wait for the interpretation. Well, it would seem that The Hague does not sit very well with you, because my understanding was that you were not too well the last time you were here, but let's move on. Reading back the transcript from the day before yesterday, you did not recollect what you had said while you were testifying in the Milutinovic trial, and yet in the statement, the additional statement of the 19th of February of this year, you managed to recollect events that were ten years ago. But am I correct if I claim that it is easier to recollect events that were sooner rather than earlier on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you're correct when you say that it is easier to recollect events of two years ago than now, but there was nothing new that I said on this particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right. But that's something the Judges will determine, what's new and what's not. Now I would like you to give me additional information. Why did you sign that statement either at that hotel or in some park between Lada and Slavija? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, please explain this to us. Tell us how this transpired, this signing of the statement. Where did you meet? How did you meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we agreed to meet at Hotel M, and the intersection when you go from Slavija towards the Zvezda stadium, there was some kind of accident. So we moved from there, and we went to a park there. We sat on a bench, and we signed the statement. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that one of the investigators who was with you on the first day was there on this occasion and some other woman who had not been there the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, neither of these individuals had been there the first time when I gave my statement, so these were not the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In other words, on this second occasion these people were new people that you hadn't seen before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had never seen them. I just signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now tell me this: Who, in addition to you, who else signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm sorry, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move on -- or, actually, let's pick up where we left off on Monday. Am I correct in saying that the only time that you used the can with aerosol, the air-freshener can, was in the house that you set on fire, that you described in paragraph 36, and that this did not repeat, this did not happen again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was in the house in Cabrat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me who was the person who used this aerosol can?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly, but I think it was Lekic. I think it's him, but I'm not sure. I've already said. I think it was him, either him or Mali, one of the two of them. But which one I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report to anyone that this house was set on fire for no reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you consider this to be normal procedure, a normal thing to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, why would I go reporting it when Nesovic was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Regardless of who was there, everyone has a duty to report a criminal act, especially a criminal act committed during wartime, regardless of who is present and who is attending.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not report it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that when you got to the third house and when the policeman was wounded, that the bombing began. Can you please describe where these bombs fell and what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bombs were falling all around, starting from the church, which is towards the end, and then the streets where we were. Some small tiny streets, we found it very difficult to go through them. Electrical poles were falling down and walls were coming down, bricks. That part was bombed, then I think that it was bombed once again after that. But that was practically the centre of Djakovica. Am I speaking too quickly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're just on the verge of being too quick, but Mr. Djurdjic is doing a good job of pausing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree with me that the military police submitted criminal charges against all the persons it found had committed criminal acts and submitted them to the military prosecutor's office for further procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right or am I correct when I say that in your unit strict discipline was imposed and that all those who perpetrated crimes were detained and handed over to the court authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. There was knowledge about all those who had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your previous statements you mentioned proceedings against Major Radic and Major -- and Lieutenant-Colonel Micic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for Major Radic, there was a criminal report submitted. As for Lieutenant-Colonel Micic, the proceedings were completed in Belgrade recently, and he was acquitted. I was there during the inquiry. Even then there weren't enough arguments for his sentencing. But in any case he was taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the legal procedures were conducted, military legal procedures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the investigation, conducted by investigators from the military police in Prizren until the time that he was brought into custody, the proceedings were conducted in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at Exhibit P962. This is on the 65 ter list. Just one moment. I would like to give you another exhibit. This is a Defence exhibit. I apologise. I find it a bit difficult to find it. It doesn't matter. Well, let's find it after the break. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mention an Exhibit 962, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P962, according to the 65 ter list. The Defence also tendered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll keep looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can look at it after the break, perhaps. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I can assist, it's 65 ter number 00962. It's not an exhibit yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That might help. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My associate did find it, Your Honours, but it's not a problem. Perhaps it's in the e-court. We will find it after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's it. Can we look at this exhibit now? Can we look at paragraph 124 and 103 first? Page 10. Page 11, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you see number 124?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please zoom in a little bit on this line, 124. Wonderful. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, is this criminal report pertaining to Slobodan Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at paragraph 104 now. This is on page 9. 104, please. Can we zoom in on that. 103, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is Zlatan Mincic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this exhibit, the whole document because these are all the persons who were criminally charged and processed in the 549th Motorised Brigade in this time period indicated in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I could find some other people here if I were to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00035, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, so we don't have to go back to this document and open it again, can you look at column 70. This should be either on page 5 or 6 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bravo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says Ivan Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. No, no. All right, I'm going to look at this later about that bridge. Well, let's continue. Thank you. Is that the soldier who killed, who actually killed that young man, but then he was later killed? It has to do with the killing under the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. Well, that boy was killed, that young man was killed later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to look at 41, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's incorrect in paragraph 41 when it is stated that your unit, "my unit had the task of ordering Albanian villagers to leave their homes," and then it goes on to say that this was ordered by Major Vlatko Vukovic, and that this usually was conveyed through Nesovic and that an order several times came directly from Vukovic. Do you agree that this is incorrectly stated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not an order. We can interpret it --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please. Now we can talk about that later. I am asserting, just tell me whether what is said here is incorrect in your statement or not. I read that. If you need, take paragraph 41 and tell me if this is an incorrect interpretation of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did tell them to go. If you consider that to be an order, then it's an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have quoted what is said in the statement. I am asking you if this is an incorrect interpretation of your words, and if it is, then we're going to establish later what is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it does say "order," then I disagree that it's an order. In my view it's not an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So, then, you agree with me that what I read to you actually is incorrectly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that's what it says. If it says an order, then that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us continue. In that paragraph it is correctly said "My Major Vukovic never issued an order about expelling the villagers," that they should be expelled to Albania. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. He never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct when I say that the population was not moving, or they did not relocate, until cluster bombs began to fall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you a part of the paragraph 41: "I claim that it is incorrectly interpreted in the statement what I am going to read now: 'Orders always referred to only the Albanian villages. I'm sure there were never any written orders for these kind of assignments. We Serbs learned in mistakes made during the wars in Croatia and Bosnia so that the commander would not order the expulsion of innocent Albanian civilians in written form but would issue a verbal, an oral, order. I'm convinced that the order came from the top, from above. This could not be an order by a local commander such as Major Vukovic, or even a brigade commander such as Delic. He could not take it upon himself to order the expulsion of civilians from the village because there is no operative goal to that. An order of that scale had to have been approved from the top.'"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note, we do not have the original statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You listened carefully to what I read from paragraph 41 of your statement, so I kindly request, if you understood my question, to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood the question, and it's like this --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, witness, just tell me if something is different than what you thought, but mainly it is the way it was put in writing. You didn't say it the way it was put in writing in the statement in that way, and then later you will say what you thought and how you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the facts is that it is not correct, that it was only the Albanians who were there. There were also some Serbs there. Let's look at the village of Brekovac, for example. There were not only Albanians there but also Serbs, and we also moved them closer to town. Nobody ordered the expulsion of those people but only their relocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, we have a large problem here because one statement of yours that is written is going to be tendered into evidence, and it is believed that what is written in correct. And in the beginning you gave the solemn declaration that this is correct. This is why I'm reading this to you, because you are under oath, to say if this statement was interpreted correctly or not, yes or no. And then later we will establish if it isn't correctly interpreted, what is correct and what is not. I'm asking you this. We have to clarify this. Do you understand? Because this is your statement. It will remain. And if it is standard, it will constitute evidence, and what you say has to be interpreted according to the law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I go ahead? Oh, I wasn't sure if you had finished or not. I said earlier that it is one thing to talk about relocation. To an extent it's correct, and to an extent it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to move now to paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I also claim that your statement was not interpreted correctly, and you can tell me if I am correct or not. Now I am quoting: "That exception actually did not apply to Kosovo. There was no legitimate reasons to relocate civilians, but we were still given the order to carry out this task. For us, from a military aspect, the expulsion of civilians didn't have any -- make any sense. While the civilians were in their homes, we were not bombed by NATO, but within a few days after they left, we were bombed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I did say that, but let me clarify why. May I do that? I, as a soldier, when the civilians were there, as a soldier I believed that it was better for them to be with us. It's up to the commander what he thinks about that. My opinion and the opinion of the commander do not have to be the same. That is the essence of what I said. I, as a soldier, feel better if the civilians are around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, may I conclude that these are your thoughts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier you said that I was correct when I said that civilians began to leave their homes only when NATO began bombing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Some left on their own. We told others to relocate. But I really cannot explain that now. If you go to somebody and you tell them something, we don't know if they consider that to be an order or not. I mean, if you come to them with a rifle - and a soldier doesn't go anywhere without a rifle - it can be interpreted as an order. I mean, I don't know, I can't explain that in any way. But in any case we were telling them that they need to go into the direction of Djakovica, not towards the border and not to go out of Kosovo, not to leave Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that when you relocated the command post from Zub, immediately after that Zub was bombed and it was flattened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not the place where our command was but the surrounding homes, yes, they were flattened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're talking about the village houses in Kosovo and Metohija, could you describe to us what a village home or house looks like in ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on whether it's a Catholic house or a Muslim house, because there is a key difference. If it is a Catholic house, it's a usual house like anywhere, with a small fence around it, but if it's a Muslim house, it has very high walls, and it's surrounded by the walls all around. These are quite large houses. There's only a few houses that you would find that are small. And there are lots of auxiliary buildings in the compound, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the outside do they have high walls surrounding them, and how high?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: High walls, at least 2 metres high. Not lower than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, do these houses have openings for rifles above the gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if these were openings for rifles, but the fact is that they have very small windows, and this is especially particular for villages. I don't know what the reason is. And I just remember something. There's still vendetta in Kosovo, and that could be one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But will tell me now, so when you look onto a house from a street, you cannot see a window from which you can see into the house from the street; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I assume that's because of the women or for some other reason, I don't know. But that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not asking you about the reasons; I'm just asking you about the fact itself. So there is never a window on a house facing the street.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't have to be a rule, but yes, many houses are like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I was asking you about Muslim houses. You described what Catholic houses or other non-Muslim houses are like, regardless of the ethnic background of the owners, but let's move on. Can we conclude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, it's time, I'm afraid. We're going to have to have the first break now, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 4.00. We'll go into closed session so that the witness can leave.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, to wrap up this topic, am I correct when I say that Albanian village houses were a very well-fortified -- very well fortified for armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you're completely right, and I will explain now. For instance, the three villages that were encircled that we were talking about, for instance, in Meja, the houses were exactly as you said now. In Korenica they were a bit different, a bit more modern, whereas in Brekovac the houses are totally modern. They do have high wall fences, but they are completely different to the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume that we've clarified and made a distinction between the village houses that weren't Muslim as opposed to Catholic or other houses, so I'm just asking about the Muslim houses not about the Catholic houses that you've already explained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my answer is the same as I've already said. It depends on the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any first-hand experience where -- with people barricaded inside a Muslim village house with these high walls? If you did, please tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we consider those three houses that we entered in Cabrat, you could interpret it as such, regardless of the fact that they were in a town --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please listen to me, Witness. Did you have any armed clash or experience with one of -- with a house like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult. There is only one entrance into the compound. There are these huge high walls. Once you walk into the yard, it's almost like a room. So if there is someone in the house and you are in the yard, there is no chance that you can defend yourself. Are you satisfied?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, and if the gate is closed? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult to enter into the yard. For instance, if this was somewhere in the centre of a village, there is a wall behind you, and you never know whether there's anybody else on the other side of the wall, so it was a very, very unpleasant situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that your statement was incorrectly interpreted in paragraph 45 where it is stated, in the first sentence, in the first line: "After the entire village -- after we had ordered the village to leave within an hour, it was like an atom bomb had hit the village. Soldiers would go through the village and loot anything that wasn't nailed down. They took things that they could not even imagine they were going to be able to take them home to Serbia. There is a lot more that I could say about the looting that went on."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you haven't completed the entire statement. I also mentioned that this was perpetrated by individuals, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, first, please, I'm asking you about this portion that is in the statement. Was this correctly interpreted or not? Was this the context in which you put it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a conversation between me and the investigator, but the context is that this was done by individuals. This was not an organised action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is not about context; this is your statement. And if it remains as is, then there is no other explaining it. So I'm just asking you: Was this properly interpreted as stated here in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I told you that in the end I said that this was perpetrated by individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, forget about the individuals. Just tell me, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, not about the organisation. The bomb -- as if a bomb had fallen and that you hadn't done anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did see this. I saw it myself. But, sir, the men that did this, they wore uniforms, but they weren't members of our unit. I assert this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell -- are you telling me that you saw some other members of some other units that stole or looted during the war and that you did not arrest them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them, certainly, but I did not arrest anyone. Just to be clear, I did not arrest anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did you see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw this on a number of occasions, but, as I said, this was perpetrated by individuals. These individuals were sometimes civilians, both of Serbian ethnicity and Albanian. Now, if you can show me the paper that you showed me earlier where all those names were listed, there should be on those lists some women, Albanian women, who also were arrested because they, too, looted, not to mention the Roma people. They carried away anything they could. They took away washing machines and anything they could get hold of. So I think this was looted by members of units -- or the unit that was there but not our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me you are not really listening to my question in this portion of the statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, I did. I know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, here it says: "After we had ordered the villagers to leave within an hour, it was like an atom bomb had hit the village."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that this was done by members of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, then, that you did not order the villagers to leave their villages and that that is not the substance of paragraph 45? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, here it says "ordered." I told the Prosecutor that the word "order" could not be translated in any other way. We told these people to leave and go towards Djakovica. One thing is to issue an order to someone and force them to do something, and it's quite a different thing when you just tell someone to go somewhere. I don't know what the reason was, and it wasn't my place to ask about the reasons, but we told these people, You should go to Djakovica and find houses where you could stay with maybe members of your extended family or relatives. So the order was not to the effect that they should move out to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to go about this. I told you what was stated in your statement. You said, "After we had ordered the villagers to leave within an hour," and now you're saying you didn't order them. Is it correct that you didn't order them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for me, it was not an order, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That means that this was not correctly translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I told the Prosecutor that this was not an order, but it couldn't be translated in any other way into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, forget the investigator, but, you see, English is a very complex and rich language, and there would be a way of translating it. So this, what is stated here, that you had ordered, that was not something that you actually said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, an order is something quite different. It is when you clearly state to someone, You must do so and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel and witness please slow down. The interpreters cannot keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at paragraph 47. All right, 47. You state here in paragraph 47 that five policemen were ambushed and killed. Tell me, were you an eye-witness to this? Did you hear of this? How did you learn of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about this. I saw their boots at the health centre. I took some soldiers for an examination, a medical examination, at the health centre there. It was an improvised sort of hospital there. And people were saying that these were boots that were worn by the policemen who had gone on patrol earlier in the morning, or, rather, not on patrol but towards the check-point, towards Junik. I don't know exactly where that check-point was. Whether it was an ambush or not, I don't know, but they went -- they went that way. They patrolled that road every single day. But there was no army in that village at the time, so in fact they were killed by a hand-held launcher, rifle launcher, and all that remained were boots and some parts of some equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said they fired at them and shot them or hit them. Who was it? Who fired at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who else it could be if not KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You then go on to state that a few days after this event, 400 policemen came.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How do you know that this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do I know? Well, they came on buses because they were not from Djakovica. They were not stationed in Djakovica at this point so they came from somewhere. The police station in Djakovica had a certain number of policemen. Some of them were at check-points; some were on the premises. But these people came from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's just be brief. You said they came. Tell us how they came and where they were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came on buses from the direction of Djakovica, going towards Meja and Korenica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat his question. The interpreter did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've got so far ahead, there's a whole question been missed, we're being told. You're speaking again in a very excited manner, Mr. Djurdjic, and the witness is replying in an even more excited manner, and neither of you are leaving a break between question and answer at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where were you, Witness, when you say that you saw these buses with policemen on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is I was at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where was this command post, and what time period are we talking about, or approximately just the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the month of the events -- I'm not sure of the date, but I think this was in April. No, I'm sure it was in April. This was on the road leading from Djakovica to Junik. So they were going from Djakovica to Korenica and Meja, those two villages. Between the crossroads and Korenica, our command post was somewhere between the crossroads and the road to Djakovica, but not the command post. It was a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, how did you know from where you were where these buses stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, simply put, as you go uphill from the crossroads on the way to Meja, about 1 kilometre beyond that point the buses cannot go any further. They stop there; they have to come back. So in Korenica, before they got in, the policemen got off the buses, the buses turned around and left empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm not asking you about the Meja and Korenica events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the 400 policemen that I mentioned there because I had not seen them before. I saw them on this occasion. Before that they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, please, now I will read out to you paragraph 47. This has nothing to do with the policemen you are talking about. We're not talking about Korenica and Meja. That will come a little later. My question referred to this paragraph, that five policeman were ambushed and killed, and that because of this incident, 400 police officers came to Djakovica. So if you are now talking about Meja, then that would mean that the interpretation in paragraph 47 is also incorrect, and that's why I'm asking you about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The paragraph reads: "About 400 additional police arrived in the Djakovica area in about 10 buses ..." not "arrived in Djakovica."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in Djakovica, not in the area of Djakovica, and it's not just 400 policemen, there are more. But this is on their arrival in Djakovica, and only in the following -- in the paragraphs that follow will there be mention of the events that the witness was talking about. So what I'm asking him about is:

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that so many policemen and troops arrived in Djakovica, before the events in Meja and Korenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, it does not say in paragraph 47 that they arrived in Djakovica; it says "in the Djakovica area" and that is correct. They came to the Djakovica area, not the town itself. But of course they did have to go through the town. They couldn't get through any other way. There is only one bridge that they could have crossed. There was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to be forced now to read. This is the sentence in -- let me see, the third sentence: "Within days after this incident about 400 additional police arrived in Djakovica in about 10 buses and a number of civilian vehicles." So in Djakovica, I just read it to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 47, the third sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my copy it says the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, the fourth sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Within days after this incident about 400 additional police arrived in Djakovica ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are unable to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, was this wrongly cited in this statement or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we look at the word "podrucju" area, then that is not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not there. The word "podrucju" is not there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if this refers to the days that preceded --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It only refers to the day of that event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, the English translation has the word "area," qualifying Djakovica. I cannot speak for the other version. But your cross-examination is proceeding on the basis that there's no word "area" there. The two versions appear to be on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian it says "in Djakovica" or "to Djakovica." There's no word "area" in the fourth sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's just far too, far too fast, and you weren't speaking into the microphone. The witness accepts, Mr. Djurdjic, that in the Serbian language there is no word "area," but it's in the English version. That may be enough for your purposes. You may now need to find out whether the witness is meaning "in the town itself" is or is meaning "in the area of the town."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct, Your Honour. In the English version, I just looked, it does say "area." That is correct. What I'm interested in is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, please listen carefully. Does this refer to the time before the events in Korenica and Meja, or you are thinking of the day when they came to Korenica and Meja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please, you have to say which one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only to the day they came to Meja and Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a general kind of question for you now. Am I correct if I were to say that during the war in Kosovo and Metohija in 1999, there were no paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guarantee - I guarantee - that as far as the area I was in, for sure there was no such soldier there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or members of anything. If anyone would have appeared with anything, they would have been arrested for sure. There's no question of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My next question would now refer to a part of your statement where you mention -- it's the same paragraph, Frenki's men. Am I correct when I say that you saw two persons with a hat that you say when you saw them before were worn by Frenki's men, but you don't know to which units those two members or those two persons belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I spoke with them. We exchanged -- I had cigarettes. They gave me juice. They were driving some private cars, and they told me they were members of the JSO. What it says here, that they were Frenki's men, I don't know how they turned out there. I did not see other members of that unit, except for those two people. I don't know how they happened to come there. I didn't see any other members of that unit, other than those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I then can conclude that you told the investigator that these were members of the JSO, but that he intentionally didn't put that in, but he put in that Frenki's men were there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was your answer to that, please, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the JSO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mention Frenki's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I know that these were -- this was the JSO unit. Why would I call them Frenki's men? This is not a private army. It's a part of the -- part of the Ministry of the Interior. What is the name? At the time it was called -- I don't know what it was called, the State Security, actually. Is that how it was? I think I said that correctly but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, the person who conducted the interview arbitrarily put this term in, "Frenki's men," of his own will; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when we're talking about the people who questioned you, and there were a few of them there, did anybody introduce themselves as a military or a police expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There are many things that are strange, even concerning the translation of what I wanted to say. Well, let me not go into that, let me not take up too much of your time, but the most controversial situations have to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, let us continue. Let us move to this paragraph 48. I assert that in this paragraph what is incorrectly entered is that you stated that your unit surrounded the area around the villages of Korenica and Meja --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that it surrounded the villages. I just said it blocked one part of the road Korenice-Djakovica-Junik between the intersection of Korenica and a part of the creek which goes towards that same -- from that same intersection toward the village of Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, you're putting the question instead of me, but let us assert, it means that this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise, but this is a quotation here, which I just wanted to bring on the record. The question was that, in paragraph 48, it was incorrectly stated that "your unit surrounded the area around the villages of Korenica and Meja," and I'm just reading here from the English version, which is signed by the witness, and it says that "the VJ, including my unit, received the order to surround and secure the area around the villages of Korenica and Meja." Receiving an order to surround is certainly different than surrounding the unit -- than surrounding the locations itself. I just wanted to bring this on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree, especially because I have a certain opinion about the statement that is being tendered and admitted here under 92 ter, and it's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My next question will be: Am I correct that you said to the investigator that your unit received an assignment to carry out a blockade of the village from Korenica towards the village of Meja-Orize?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A blockade, yes, because with the number of people that we were participating with at the time, you couldn't surround such a territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you're a trained professional, so the difference between surrounding, or encircling, or blockading; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In this indictment it is constantly stated that the villages were surrounded by the forces of the Army of Yugoslavia and the police. That is why I'm putting this question to you. This is stated in the indictment by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just say something now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about the blockade of the road between the intersection that I mentioned and the village of Korenica. A part of the creek also was blockaded by a part of my unit. As for what was on the other side, I don't know because I didn't see that. I don't know if there were any other members there of anything, of the police or the army. I didn't see that. But it is a fact that a number of the police came from the direction where our blockade was not located.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at a document of the Prosecution under the 65 ter list, P number 615.4, on the screen, please. Thank you. Better. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you be able to mark with an X the place where the command post was that you came to when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I can mark on the map, or I can make a marking without this part here. I know that road really well. I am very familiar with that road. You just tell me the place where the command was for that day. That's what you're talking about. It's on the road, in order to be able to write the letter -- well, that's why I put the little circle here. The house is right next to the road. Was I clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Next to this little circle can you please place the letters "KM," "komandno mesto," command post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, now, please, can you mark the line of the blockade of your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From here, from the intersection, the intersection, up to here, approximately up to the entrance of the village, and then this part of the creek, somewhere from here, somewhere along here, in this area. I apologise, I am not very good at drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of these arrows can you please put the number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, where -- there and on this other side, where you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is for the transcript, just to note that at the end of line of blockade, the witness placed the number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to mark the place where the police check-point was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also on the intersection itself, but farther away than I actually meant to draw it in. The pen is not very precise, but it's somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No problem. You can place the number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the houses that happened to be close to the check-point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indicated -- well, actually, it's a bit imprecise. The check-point was here, the houses were here, more or less. Is it clear now? The check-point was on the intersection itself, and the houses are some 30 to 40 metres away from the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At the end of that line, can you please mark the number 3. Number 3 will be the location where those houses were located close to the check-point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you something else. Was there something else there that you are able to mark; and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were houses here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark that place with the letter K.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me who came to the location where the blockade was together with you, and at what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 6.00 in the morning and Srdjan Kostic was with me from my squad and some other active-duty soldiers. I don't know what their names were. I don't remember if the commander came with us or if he came later. I'm not quite sure about that. But I think that it was about 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came on foot, and I think that the commander came in an ambulance. I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where did you set off from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Brekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who told you to go to Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: that we were supposed to go towards Korenica and that we would find an abandoned house there and that we were supposed to wait there. That was the day before we actually went there, the evening before we went.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day we all set off there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who did you report to before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You were told by the commander of the squad that you were supposed to go there. Who did you report to? Who did you set off with so that they would know that you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went with a part of the command platoon there. We all left Brekovac together, that part of the command platoon and some other soldiers from our unit. I don't know, actually, where the others were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you, who did you report to that you were supposed to leave to Korenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the morning. When your commander told you that you had to go to Korenica, he wasn't with you. Who did you report to? Who did you set off to go to Korenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to the intersection together. Later then he went in the direction of Meja, and we stayed there at the abandoned house. This happened the following morning, not when we received our order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I asked him whom did he inform in the morning that he was going to Korenica and who did he set out for Korenica with, not that he had received the order in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we all set off together. I can't tell you exactly how many of us there were. There were quite a few. Maybe some 50 or 60 men. Maybe more. I can't tell you the exact number, but we all went there together, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who led this group that set off then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall. One of the officers from the command, but I can't recall who. But not Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in the area where the command post was supposed to be, did you search the surrounding terrain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because this was an old dilapidated house. It was deserted. It must have been deserted 30 years earlier. There was nothing. It was just ruins, an old ruined house, in ruins, and there was an auxiliary small shed or building, so there was no need to search.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the unit -- the part of the unit that went to set up the blockade, did they search the terrain before they took up the positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because this was right next to the house. They were just on the other side of the road where they set up positions, so they were just there one by one. They were about 10 to 15 metres, one from another, and that's how it was. So there is no need to search the terrain when the road was completely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you just mark the spot where soldier Letic was in this blockade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot indicate precisely the spot, but it was approximately in this area, this line towards the creek. I can't recall exactly now, but I'm sure it was in this part. He was next to the creek or up the creek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark -- put an L there to the right side of the creek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, how far is it from the command post to the crossroads where the check-point was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not more than 120 metres. Maybe less, but let's say it was 120 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So if that was the case, then from that check-point to Meja, it was about 40 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, sir. From the check-point to Meja it was about -- well, it was uphill. Let me think. I can't really assess exactly, but at least 600 to 700 metres from that spot to the first houses. Maybe even 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, then, on the way to Orize, what was the terrain like and how far was it from the check-point to Orize?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know because I never was -- I never was in Orize. I know it was uphill, and I know that you could get to Meja, to the approaches to Meja on a bus, and then after that you can't because there are a lot of walls, huge rock walls, and you couldn't get through there on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, could you see from the command post Meja and could you see Orize?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the beginnings of the Meja village but not Orize, because Orize was behind Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the way I see it, Meja was to the east of the command post, whereas Orize was to the north.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, listen, it doesn't matter how it's drawn up here on the map. I was in those villages, and I know exactly what it looked like. So as you go uphill, Meja remains on this side, and then you go to Orize. So it's not the road going by Meja, it is through Meja, and then you get to Orize.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you, but we have a map here in front of us, and you won't argue that this map is incorrect, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, but I'm just telling you about the road to Orize from Meja. There's only that one road going through Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I was asking you about this map, and I asked you to mark this map, whether the configuration was correct and whether it's correct, the way these villages are indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it would be correct if a road was shown going through Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, regardless of the road, is the village put in the right place here in the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If it is all right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see the village of Meja is here and Orize is here, and you can see the road going by the village. So here's Meja and here's Orize, but the road goes, in other words, through Meja and through Orize; it connects them, and then it goes on. But there were also some Serbian houses here at the beginning of the village, not just at the beginning but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I would now like to take you to paragraph 60 in the Serbian version. In this paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you planning to tender this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes. I seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00036, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 60 that -- and I'm referring to the sentence, penultimate sentence, it says, under quotation marks, between quotation marks, it says "slaughtering Siptars." After all this time, I know everything you've said about this, but am I right that this word, "slaughtering Siptars," was not properly interpreted and that it should not be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Now I would like to point you to paragraph 65.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still see the map on the screen so I don't see the paragraphs. I don't see what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 65. Don't we have it on the screens? Could I please -- Mr. Registrar, could we have on the screens paragraph 65 of his statement in Serbian, because I can see that the map is still on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please just enlarge it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the sentence before last in the statement, it says, in your written statement: "These men, like the others before, were made to sing some Serbian nationalistic songs."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say "like the others before," I said "only this group."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So it is not correctly written down in the statement, what you had said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said literally "only this last group."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So what's in the statement, what we've just read, that's incorrect; right? "These men, like the others ..." that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the words "like the others before" shouldn't be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct that you stated that you had seen four groups of men and that in the last group alone, there were eight to ten men; whereas the other groups were a little smaller, two to three men each?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in the Milutinovic trial you said that those men were between 22, 23, and 30 years of age, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Referring to the last group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my assessment, so this is just an approximation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was the distance between the command post and where he was, the spot where he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, because I don't know exactly the spot where he was exactly. I know -- I don't know where he was assigned, to what spot exactly. I know where our squad was, approximately the area from which it should have been up to where, but I don't know exactly what position he was at and where he was wounded, where he was exactly when he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't hear you, so how far was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because I don't know where exactly he was, and I never said that I saw the spot where he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So I can conclude that you never went to the spot where he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wanted to make a friendly announcement, and I've fallen in the same trap before. My learned friend is mentioning a couple of colleagues of this witness who is protected, and I believe the more we keep on mentioning the witness's direct or immediate colleagues in open session, the easier it will be to identify this witness. If I could just kindly ask my colleague to go into private session when he addresses such issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Those references have been redacted, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is totally irrelevant that anyone could hear that. I have absolutely no reason to hide from anyone. I don't care at all whether it's an open session or a closed session, and I don't have any concerns about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will continue to preserve the confidentiality --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have no fears about any threats, especially not any threats from General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to thank my learned friend Mr. Neuner, because I got carried away, but I have another difficulty here. Yesterday, at the very beginning of the evidence of this witness, Lieutenant Nesovic was mentioned, his name, and then Vukovic, not to mention the brigade, so I proceeded from the belief that there were already some indications there, some identifying points mentioned. But yes, we could go into closed session, and I won't mention any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just another question. You said -- how far did you say it was from the command post to the crossroads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said not more than 120 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And from the crossroads to the positions where the blockade was? Because it was towards Orize, uphill, obviously, how far was it from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly. If we assume that it was about 10 to 15 metres and that they -- between men and that they took up exactly the positions they were supposed to, so then it would have been about 120 metres, uphill, towards the village, if they were all in the same area, if they took up their positions exactly as they should, assuming that the distance between soldiers was about 10 to 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, Witness, now, looking at paragraph 62 of your statement, where you stated that Branislav Letic, when he was wounded, the ambulance wasn't even there, that it only came later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the yard throughout this time, except when they took Letic away to the field hospital and when the other two men were taken. I can't recall their names, but I know them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I will quote you, and that's in the one-before-last sentence: "No sooner than the ambulance returned to the hospital," so the ambulance went to the hospital. It wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it probably took those two previous wounded men to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Do you agree with me that the task of your part of the unit in this blockade was to prevent the KLA from moving or withdrawing from the area that you were blocking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that for the execution of this assignment your commander formed three execution squads and engaged a platoon of the military police, communications, and the medics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I said, more or less. I gave you the number of soldiers who were there before we came. That would be that more or less between 60, 70, or 100 people. I don't believe that there were so many.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the documents that we have, it can be concluded that the movement to Korenica began at 3.30, and that by 6.00 in the morning the line of blockade was taken up. Am I correct, or do you believe that I'm not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really say. Perhaps you are correct. I don't know exactly what time it was, but we were at our positions by 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the line of blockade was taken up and that the length was some 2 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you take Orize from Meja and this part, I don't know if it's 2 kilometres or not. I'm not sure that it was that long. It's too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. But am I correct when I say that your unit did not stop and check civilians and that in no way did it force the population to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
