utterances.text: You are correct, but let's just clarify about those 2 kilometres. Perhaps if the number of people who were in the houses close to the road towards Korenica, perhaps you could get that number and then put it together and you can get 2 kilometres, but that's not that. The blockade was not that long. But I do agree with what you said last.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to evidence presented in this case or documents in this case, on the 28th, the second day, at 2.00 your platoon of the military police was attacked in the area of Kodra e Kikes and the terrorists tried to pull out towards Djakovica and that they were prevented from doing that. Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the blockade at that time, too, and I didn't hear any firing, and I don't know anyone. We were in the blockade, and I don't know who was supposed to come and -- well, now, something was happening over there between the civilian police and someone over there. I don't know why we were doing this blockade. It's probably that nobody would come out. But not military because, sir, our military police platoon, our military police did not have the authority to cross over the other side of the river. It could not have been attacked. It didn't cross the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I am asking you, please, to listen to me carefully. I'm reading slowly to you. So what I asked you was like this: The next day, not the day you came there but the following night, at 2.00 in the morning, am I correct if I say that your military police platoon was attacked that was in the area of Kodra e Kikes, in the area of Capta, and that terrorists tried to pull out along that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct if I were to say that Lieutenant Nesovic was the security officer in the 2nd Motorised Battalion and that he did not command any unit and could not have been in command of the unit where you were either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, he was a security organ over there. We said we shouldn't mention any names, but you mentioned them anyway. But it doesn't matter. My squad was directly under his command, so he was directly in command of my squad, not the lieutenant second class who was in the 2nd Platoon of the military police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question. The interpreters didn't get it. And you're also touching upon an area, you're talking about the squad in which the witness was, which is sensitive in terms of his identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Neuner, I did not actually specify the squad but the unit. The witness mentioned the squad in his answer, which I have no influence about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But my question or assertion was that the commander of the battalion - I don't want to tell his name and we know who that is - had the authority to command that unit and that's what he was doing and that was what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps the commander did command, but he did it through -- I mean, the orders were issued by the lieutenant. I don't want to mention his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, or I would like to assert that the location where the command was, because of the configuration of the terrain, you were not able to see the entry -- the entrance to Korenica and those houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I know that road really well. I went along that road several times, not during the war. I'm talking about the time before the war. So that part of the road, from our command post to the first houses in Korenica, is completely flat or straight. There is no forest or woods on the side of the road. On the left side there are fields. On the right side is some kind of hillock. But the actual road is completely flat and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me whether you can see the village of Deva from that command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Parts of the village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see the road leading from the village of Deva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I assert that from your command post, because of the configuration of the terrain, you could not see the road leading from Deva, and in order to get there you would need to cross to the -- you needed to cross the Renik river in order to reach your command post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the road, from the road, from Deva, is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And to pass through the combat disposition through the Renik river in order to reach your command post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whose combat disposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your unit that was in the blockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, that part of the road from our command post up to the first houses on the left side, on the riverbank, there is a clear field, a totally flat field. You can see almost every house practically. I don't know the name of all the villages, but I know that on the left side of the Djakovica-Junik road, that part that we're talking about, the left side is totally flat. There's a flat field there. Do you know what that means? A totally flat field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I still assert that you were not able to see civilians who were coming from the village of Rogovo, Kusnin? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we are talking about -- sir, are you talking about people who were -- are you maybe thinking about villages that are on the other side of that river, that are not on the side that we're talking about? There's a river, and they're on the other side of the river. Well, those people were not even there then. They left before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So I'm right, and you didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right, all right. We'll see that later. But you did say you didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. But, I mean, they were not there, so how could I have seen them? If we're talking about the villages that were on the other side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, you heard what I was saying and what I was telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just want to bring on a record, because a couple of locations have been suggested to this witness in the past minutes, whether these locations would be visible from the command post, I, myself, was a little bit confused. It was started out by clear sight or visibility of the village of Korenica and then a couple of new houses -- sorry, new villages were suggested. I personally found that very confusing, and I didn't really know what my learned colleague wanted to establish. As far as I remember, the witness has only testified about visibility of Korenica and Meja and not of the other places suggested by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought at one point that the village mentioned was Deva, D-e-v-a, according to the transcript. It may be Meja, but it appeared to be Deva. But otherwise we don't know which villages. The evidence of the witness appears to be that in that direction, persons could be seen on his side of the river, but he doesn't suggest that persons could be seen on the other side of the river.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me clarify the situation. The Defence counsel says -- or he's talking about some places whose names I don't know, but there is a village by the river on this side, the village from which I took civilians to Djakovica. I, myself, and another soldier from Sombor, pursuant to an order from Commander Vukovic, because they had already started to come out of their houses. They were afraid, and they started to come out of their houses. I took them personally. This is what I assert. This is pursuant to the commander's command. I can ask him; you can ask him. We can confront each other. He literally told me, These people have to leave. You have to take them there, and you are responsible to me for their safety. That's it, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if it's time for a break. I would still have 10 to 15 minutes at the most, depending on how quickly I will get my answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can go a little longer because we were late starting, but would you prefer to have a break now so that you can collect your thoughts? We will resume at ten past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and thank you to the witness for confirming what he said and that was without my question. This was actually the thrust of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But now we need to be efficient. Can you please tell me, at what time did you get information that two of your soldiers were wounded when you were at the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to see the place of the wounding from the command post where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into closed session, please, because I need to mention some things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you briefly about the relocation of villagers from places south of Djakovica. Could you tell me, when you were coming to the doors of these houses, were you in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And were you armed when you were talking to the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How -- when you told the people to leave the villages, were you informing them that people had a choice, whether to stay or whether to leave, or what exactly did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they should go towards Djakovica, that they should head for Djakovica. I can't describe this. It wasn't an order, but it wasn't a request either. When somebody comes into your yard with a weapon, it's a very unpleasant situation, both for the person issuing such an order and the person who has to actually comply with it. But it wasn't -- they weren't under threat of weapons to relocate, because for me expulsion or relocation would be the case where we would come there with weapons and order them to leave to Albania and not to move just a kilometre or half a kilometre away to another hamlet. And just another thing, if I may. At this time there were some parts of the police, and General Djordjevic knows about them, that had been established before the war. In some instances these people were with us. And we never forbade these civilians to go back to their homes to take their food, their staples, whatever this was they needed, their clothes, and so on. They were never prohibited from doing this. And I just want to stress that these police officers were, for the most part, Albanian, ethnic Albanians, not Serbs. I just want this to be clear. That unit was established, and it was formed, it was composed, of local Albanians. And this was not only the case in Djakovica but throughout Kosovo. I don't know if this was ever mentioned earlier here, but you can find this in state documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is, when you left these villages or hamlets, did you see that persons stayed behind or had these persons left before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for the most part we left with them, together. Not escorting them but going with them together. Sometimes with them; sometimes ahead of them. But we never escorted them. They left on their own. They went -- we told them, and they went on their home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please listen to my questions. I have a couple of questions, and I want that you finish tonight. So my question was, did you see whether families or persons stayed behind in the village when you escorted people out there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So is it correct to say that the villages were empty, once you left them with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the hamlets? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move now back to the Korenica area. You mentioned in relation to Mr. Vuckovic and Mr. Lapadatovic, that - this is page 74 of today's transcript - "fire was from the police. The police that was in the village somewhere." Which village were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm thinking of Korenica because I was in the vehicle that was fired at. I am stating that now. I stated that before, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So are you talking about fire which is coming up while you're driving in the ambulance, or are you talking about fire which is directed at the two gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither. I think that the fire just accidentally came from the fire. It was -- there was firing in that direction, but it wasn't deliberately firing at the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see where these two soldiers were wounded, but I believe that the vehicle was not shot at deliberately. The fire was coming from the village, from Korenica, but at that point in time, from those first houses where the shooting could possibly come from, there were no people there. The people had already left before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And with people having left before, you're talking about the inhabitants? Can you clarify? Inhabitants of Korenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the first houses in Korenica, because logically the houses were already burning by then. There could have been no fire coming from those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Then my learned colleague mentioned Deva and Guska. Have you -- and people leaving these two places. Have you, yourself, seen any villagers from these two locations leaving on a particular day in 1999, meaning leaving in masses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I think that -- I am practically sure that Deva and Guska are, as you go along the road from Djakovica towards Junik, you cross the river, and it's on the other side of the hill, but these people had already gone earlier, after a bombing that occurred earlier in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please listen to my question. I'm asking you, when the villagers are leaving Deva or Guska, did you, yourself, see it? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you in the broader area west of Djakovica, where these two places are located, at the point in time when the villagers from these two villages were leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see them when they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to know that you didn't see them because you told us already. I want to know whether you were in the broader area around these villages of Deva and Guska when people left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If you believe that that was the place where I was at the time, yes, if that's what you're thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So how many kilometres, roughly, were you away from people leaving these two villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, the road --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I just need a short answer, please, because I want to ask you some other questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The road from Deva and Guska passes through Brekovac. There is no other road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You're not listening to my question. I'm simply asking you how many kilometres were you away when people - what you believe and never saw - left Guska and Deva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't leave that day that we're talking about at all. This is what I'm repeating all the time. Something is wrong here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So, in fact, you don't know when exactly people from Deva and Guska ever left in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I want to come to the NATO bombardments touched upon by my colleague. While you were in the command post in Korenica in late April 1999, did NATO planes bomb your command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did NATO planes that day bomb Korenica village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did NATO planes that day bombard Meja or Orize?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If NATO would have bombarded these places - Korenica, Meja, or Orize - that day, at the end of April 1999, would you have known about this, being at the command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had there been any bombing that day, I would have known about it. It was close, close.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to take you now to the paragraph 47, the last three sentences in this paragraph 47 of your statement. You talked about JSO or Frenki's men. I think you gave my learned colleague, you talked about JSO. Could you, first of all, explain to us what JSO is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: JSO is a unit for special operations, and it was formed as -- under the auspices of the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia. One of the commanders used to be Frenki Simatovic, I think that's his name, and that's how they got their nickname, Frenkijevci. But that's not mean that that is what the unit was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly in which disposition was the State Security Service of Serbia? To which ministry did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe a uniform worn by people from the JSO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot do that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say in your statement that you met two gentlemen and exchanged cigarettes, juice, whatever, so you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but they were wearing the hats. They said -- they told me they were from the JSO, and they had the insignia of the JSO on them. But if that is recognition, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's go for the hat. Can you describe the hat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage hat. I don't know. Perhaps you can see it on some photograph or other -- the photograph, I think it's on photograph number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't want you to mention any numbers. I want you, first of all, to tell me what colour the hat has, what camouflage colour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's more yellow than -- sir, I don't know. It's been ten years since then. How can I remember? I don't know. I have a uniform like that at home, so I could, you know, in a way. But right now I just cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Then you mentioned you saw insignia, these men wearing insignia, of the JSO. Can you describe how the insignia looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Red, and then in the circle it says "JSO," and then it's something like that on the shoulder. But now, sir, at that point in time, if you think that I was looking at who was wearing what sort of insignia, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You were answering my question. We need to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit 325 on the screen, please. Sorry, 327. This is the first page, and we could also show -- yeah, you see the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is there any insignia here, insignia from the JSO?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I want to come to my last topic. Sorry, I have one further small topic. The shooting at the yard near the crossroad, you were asked by my learned colleague also about the groups being led there. Can you tell me, you explained to us, Albanians in three to four groups, were being led there. Did you ever see from this yard Albanians coming back to the road, walking from the yard back to the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My last topic is criminal reports. What you had observed that day, and you were asked by my learned colleague about the filing of criminal reports. You, yourself, have you ever filed a criminal report, while you were in the military police, in the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the persons in the military police of that 2nd Battalion who would file such criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If you are learning about events which may qualify to be put into a criminal report, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would inform my superior officer. There would be an on-site investigation, and a report would be submitted, if the perpetrator was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned the gentlemen who were in the 2nd Battalion of the military police -- sorry, who were in the military police, in the 2nd Battalion. How would they be involved in that process you're describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since we didn't have -- they would write the report. They would write the report after we notified them. We didn't have a typewriter, a computer. There was no electricity. And it was a question if anybody at our end was able to type.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So would you before or after an on-site inspection involve the gentlemen who were writing the criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First I would inform the gentlemen. They would call criminal investigation technicians to conduct an on-scene investigation. An official report would be drafted, and then the procedure would proceed pursuant to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If you learned about an incident which could be described as a murder or the war crime of a murder but which has not been performed by soldiers but by other units, whom would you inform about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My superior officer again, of course, because to be clear, in our sector where we were, we were able to arrest someone. It was known exactly how far each group's jurisdiction lay, so we had the authority to arrest people in our own sector. If we knew the perpetrator, he would be arrested and then the procedure would continue according to the usual custom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So in order to arrest the suspects or possible perpetrators, who would carry out, in your 2nd Battalion in the 549th Brigade, such an arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military police, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would your troop, the squad - and please don't mention names; we're in open session - the squad of 12 persons to which you belonged, would this squad also be in a position to carry out arrests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it was there, yes. Whoever was there from the military police platoon, they would be going to make the arrest, regardless of who was in question. When we were arresting Major Radic, the entire platoon of the military police went, and we arrested him with all the people who were around him and all the documents, the vehicles, all the basic equipment. That is how the arrest was made, and then he was taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in how many arrests did you participate in 1999, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Major Radic, Mincic, too. I don't know; I cannot remember, but seven or eight, maybe more. I cannot remember exactly, but there were arrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you also ever arrest a person who was not in the -- in your own unit but was in another force separate from the 549th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because in our sector there were no other units, just ours. The part that -- at least in the part that I was, no other units were stationed there. Actually, it's possible, but I don't think that this was recorded. Some soldiers from the anti-aircraft squad got drunk, and we arrested them. One of them is working together with me at the moment. I just remembered that. I mean, there were things like that, active-duty soldiers who got drunk, but they were not creating any disorder. They were not firing, but we arrested them because of the discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm very direct. Did you ever arrest a person from the civilian police in 1999, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you have done so, if this person was involved in serious crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our territory or area, yes, of course we could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If we go back to the day where -- in April 1999, where your command post was east of Korenica, how far was the AOR of your battalion's command post, the AOR which you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From where? How far from where? You said how far was your area of responsibility? I didn't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I can have a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We have 615.3, I believe, or 4. Yes, this is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you thinking of the command post or -- and the check-point where the policemen were?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In a way, yes. Would you consider that the check-point and the yard where the policemen were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 120 metres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And was this check-point and the yard within the AOR for which your commander was responsible that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say because, Your Honours, our battalion, its AOR ended on the river, on the left bank of the river. The Defence counsel said that the Deva and Guska villages were there. That was part of our area of responsibility. As for the other part that continued from there, I don't know. I think it was the AOR of some other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But the very specific question is: The yard where the shooting occurred, would you consider this yard to be within your AOR on that day, in late April 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But didn't the logbook entry you and my colleague -- sorry, my colleague asked you to look at, define that from Korenica, above the -- through the cemetery and the crossroad up to Kodra e Kikes was a line held by your forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you zoom in a little bit on the map, please, or zoom out, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I have an objection. From what I read in the diary, the house and the place that my learned friend is questioning the witness about is not mentioned anywhere, or that it's part of the AOR. I mean, it does not arise from that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I thought I read it out, but I think I've made the point clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I've just one question for you, Witness. Did you discuss that day with your commander about pulling the remaining 11 men from your military police squad, which were in this brook, together with you and other forces to walk into that yard and try to arrest the policemen there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, the policemen left before we withdrew, almost an hour before we did. Had we tried to arrest them, they would be dead all over the place. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: arrest and would not have permitted this from happening. But I think this was not in our area of responsibility, so he did not dare do that. I think that on this side of the river, on this side of the river where indicating right now, such an order would have been there. This side, I'm not sure that it is part of our area of responsibility, and too many dead would have occurred. I mean, we would have killed each other, the policemen and us, had there been any attempt at arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That must be the end. We have run seriously over time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know, sir, that we have managed to finish the questioning of you tonight. You are free to leave. The court officers will show you out after we have left here. Thank you for your assistance and for coming to The Hague. We now must adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, I believe in Courtroom II. I would like to thank the interpreters and other staff who've stayed back nearly an extra quarter of an hour to enable us to finish this witness. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.13 p.m.,
